newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda adjourns genocide trials in north-east city.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda adjourns genocide trials in north-east city.

text.p: A former secondary school teacher appeared in a Rwandan court on Tuesday on charges of genocide in the 1994 slaughter of Tutsis but the hearing was adjourned when the defendant requested access to a lawyer of his own choosing.

Francois Bizimana, accused of genocide and crimes against humanity, was not asked to enter a plea after he rejected the state-appointed lawyer. The Byumba High Court granted his request to pick his own lawyer and ordered that the trial start again in January but did not give a specific date.
Court officials said they did not expect any more trials to open on Tuesday, as announced earlier by Deputy Justice Minister Gerard Gahima.

The trials are part of efforts by the tiny tea and coffee-growing nation to bring to justice some 90,000 mostly Rwandan Hutus now in jail and accused of participating in the 1994 slaughter of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus. The killings broke out after the assassination of Hutu President Juvenal Habyarimana in April 1994.
But the main players in the slaughter are in living comfortably in exile in Africa, Europe and America.

Bizimana is a Category One prisoner -- a class that carries a mandatory death sentence if the defendant is found guilty and is reserved for the key planners and supervisors of the genocide. The slaughter was halted when the Tutsi rebels now in power took over the country in mid-1994.

Trials have now started in cases against five people, with the first opening on Friday in the southeastern town of Kibungo, where two men pleaded not guilty to organising massacres. Two other men appeared in court on Monday in Kigali but their cases were immediately adjourned.
In Kibungo, Deo Bizimana, a former medical assistant, and Egide Gatanazi, a former local administrator, both pleaded not guilty to organising massacres.
On Monday a court in Kigali adjourned the trial of Silas Munyageshali, a former prosecutor in Kigali, to an unnamed date in 1997 and the case was moved to the town of Gitarama south of Kigali.
A three-man panel of judges ruled it would be unfair to try Munyageshali in the same court where he previously served as prosecutor.
The trial of Theodomir Ruzirabwoba, a 50-year-old former administrator in Kigali, was adjourned until January 3 to allow victims' counsel more time to compile evidence against him.

Ruzirabwoba is accused of overseeing the massacres of minority Tutsis living in an area under his control at that time, of not preventing genocide and of personally killing those targetted during the slaughter.
Unlike the Kigali trials, which were attended by hundreds of chanting genocide survivors, the Byumba trial failed to attract the same attention and the small court room was nearly empty.
On Monday, two human rights groups hailed the start of genocide trials in Rwanda but slammed the court hearings as superficial and flawed by a lack of defence lawyers.

The Paris-based International Federation of Human Rights Leagues (FIDH) and the New York-based Human Rights Watch/Africa said they ..."welcome the holding of trials in Rwanda but deplore serious irregularities".

The FIDH and Human Rights Watch dismissed Rwanda's arguments that it lacked cash for defence lawyers, saying the U.N. had given up a project to supply lawyers in 1995 after opposition from Kigali's government.
"Political opposition is a factor as strong as the lack of funds," the rights groups said.
An exiled Hutu refugee lobby group -- the Rally for the Return of Refugees and Democracy in Rwanda (RDR) -- has also denounced Rwanda's judicial move as "kangaroo courts".

The RDR said suspects had recieved no legal counselling of their choice and had been denied the right to be tried in languages of their choice by the English-speaking administration that overthrew a French system.
